question:
A bug travels from \(A\) to \(B\) along the segments in the hexagonal lattice pictured below. The segments marked with an arrow can be traveled only in the direction of the arrow, and the bug never travels the same segment more than once. How many different paths are there?

[Figure 1](figures/2012_AMC_12B_Q22_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
The direction rule applies to every arrowhead shown, including the small solid ones. These solid arrows point rightward along their segments; the three hollow arrows on the middle horizontal line point leftward.

[Figure 1](figures/2012_AMC_12B_Q22_question_fig1.svg)

At the right endpoint of each hollow arrow, all three incident arrows point away from that vertex. The bug cannot reach such a vertex from \(A\). At the left endpoint, all three incident arrows point into the vertex, so a bug arriving there cannot continue to \(B\). Consequently no successful path uses a middle horizontal segment or any of its endpoints.

Removing those unusable middle vertices separates successful paths into two cases: paths above \(AB\) and paths below \(AB\). We can count the upper case by writing the number of paths reaching the right endpoint of each horizontal segment. At a merge, add the incoming counts: the possible final incoming segments are different, so these cases do not overlap. At a split, carry the current count to each available continuation.

There are seven successive columns of horizontal segments above \(AB\). Listing the counts from top to bottom within each column gives
\[
(1),\quad(1),\quad(1,1),\quad(1,2),
\]
\[
(3,2),\quad(5),\quad(5).
\]
Here the lower entry in the fourth column is \(1+1=2\). In the fifth column, the upper entry is \(1+2=3\), while the lower entry carries forward \(2\). These merge in the sixth column to give \(3+2=5\), and the final column carries those five paths to \(B\).

The lower half has the same branching and merging pattern, so it also contributes five paths. Every successful path belongs to exactly one of these two cases. Moreover, every usable move goes strictly rightward, so none can repeat a segment. Thus the displayed conditions give
\[
5+5=\boxed{10}
\]
paths. This is absent from the choices and conflicts with the supplied key \(\text{E}:2400\).

answerCheck.derivedAnswer: 10 paths under every displayed arrow; no listed choice.
answerCheck.reason: The actual enlarged SVG has a solid rightward arrowhead on every ordinary lattice edge and three hollow leftward arrowheads on the middle horizontal edges. The stem applies its direction rule to segments marked with an arrow, without exempting the solid style. Extracting all63 straight segments and48 vertices, and applying every displayed arrow, gives an acyclic directed graph. Each middle leftward edge begins at a vertex unreachable from A; its left endpoint is a sink for any incoming path. Consequently a successful path cannot use a middle edge or cross between the upper and lower halves. In the upper half, contract the ordinary horizontal edges. The successive nonzero path-count vectors across the branching layers are (1), (1), (1,1), (1,2), (3,2), (5), (5). At a merge add counts of its incoming paths. Thus there are five paths above the center line and, by reflection, five below:10 total. The attached coordinate/edge certificate independently verifies every extracted segment, reachability and backward path count. Every permitted path automatically avoids repeated edges because this actual directed graph is acyclic. No listed choice is10, and the keyed2400 is unsupported by the displayed rules. As a counterfactual only, treating ordinary edges as bidirectional while retaining the three hollow restrictions gives10992 edge-simple trails, also not2400; this is not a proposed repair.

edges.scope: systematic counting without repetition or omission
